role: Systems engineers, firmware developers and library maintainers use C to work close to operating-system and hardware interfaces.
technical: Static types, explicit pointers and manual resource lifetimes. Implementations commonly compile ahead of time to native code. The language does not automatically enforce bounds or ownership.
tradeoffs: Reason about allocation failure, integer overflow, bounds and cleanup on every exit. Use compiler warnings, sanitizers and parameterized interfaces. CODARIS uses C17 for native code and C compiled to WebAssembly in the browser.
exercise: Build a bounded text parser; test empty, oversized and malformed input.

role: Engine, graphics and native application developers use C++ when they need low-level control alongside reusable abstractions.
technical: Static typing, templates, deterministic destruction and RAII support resource ownership. Native code can use object-oriented, generic and functional techniques.
tradeoffs: Prefer explicit ownership and standard containers. Lifetime bugs, undefined behavior and complex build interfaces still require careful review.
exercise: Implement a file-processing tool with RAII and unit tests for failure paths.

role: Systems and infrastructure developers use Rust for components where memory safety and predictable resource ownership matter.
technical: Ownership, borrowing and lifetimes constrain aliasing in safe code. Traits and enums model interfaces and state; Result and Option make failure and absence explicit.
tradeoffs: Safe Rust prevents many memory errors, but unsafe blocks and foreign interfaces need separate auditing. Concurrency still requires sound design.
exercise: Write a command-line parser that returns structured errors without panicking.

role: Backend and platform developers use Go for network services, command-line tools and operational software.
technical: Static types, interfaces, garbage collection, goroutines and channels support compact concurrent programs. Packages and modules organize builds.
tradeoffs: Design cancellation, timeouts and ownership of shared state. A goroutine is lightweight but can still leak when blocked indefinitely.
exercise: Build a small HTTP service with bounded requests, cancellation and graceful shutdown.

role: Automation developers, analysts and backend engineers use Python for scripts, data workflows and services.
technical: Dynamic types, high-level collections and modules favor rapid iteration. Type annotations help tools but do not enforce runtime validation by themselves.
tradeoffs: Keep environments reproducible, validate boundary data and profile before optimizing. Native extensions can accelerate work but introduce their own failure modes.
exercise: Parse a CSV, validate rows and produce a reproducible summary with tests.

role: Browser and server developers use JavaScript for interactive interfaces and event-driven applications.
technical: Dynamic typing, lexical closures, prototypes, promises and modules. The host supplies APIs such as the DOM or server I/O; these are not identical across runtimes.
tradeoffs: Understand coercion and asynchronous error handling. Do not block the event loop with expensive synchronous work; validate all external input.
exercise: Build an accessible interactive list with loading, empty and error states.

role: Application teams use TypeScript to describe JavaScript interfaces and catch many mistakes before execution.
technical: Structural typing, unions, generics and control-flow narrowing add static analysis. Most type information is erased when emitting JavaScript.
tradeoffs: Types do not validate JSON at runtime. Treat network and storage values as untrusted until checked; avoid hiding uncertainty behind any.
exercise: Model a request as loading, success or failure with a discriminated union.

role: Backend and application developers use Java within the JVM ecosystem and its extensive libraries and tools.
technical: Static types, classes, interfaces, generics and exceptions. JVM implementations manage memory and commonly use just-in-time compilation.
tradeoffs: Budget heap use, close external resources deterministically and choose concurrency abstractions deliberately. Garbage collection does not close every resource.
exercise: Build a small service layer with typed inputs and tests around exception handling.

role: Service, desktop and game-tool developers use C# with the .NET ecosystem.
technical: Static typing with generics, pattern matching, LINQ and async/await. Managed memory reduces manual allocation work; IDisposable handles many external resources.
tradeoffs: Await asynchronous work, propagate cancellation and dispose resources. Nullable annotations help analysis but are not a substitute for boundary validation.
exercise: Write an asynchronous file-processing tool with cancellation and explicit errors.

role: Web application developers and automation authors use Ruby for expressive object-oriented programs and internal tools.
technical: Dynamic typing, objects, blocks and mixins support compact APIs. Ruby on Rails supplies a separate web framework around the language.
tradeoffs: Metaprogramming can obscure control flow. Keep behavior discoverable, test public interfaces and monitor dependencies.
exercise: Create a small command-line report using Enumerable and tests.

role: Statisticians, researchers and analysts use R for modelling, statistical computing and graphics.
technical: Vectors, data structures and an extensible package ecosystem support analysis. Missing values and vectorized operations are central concepts.
tradeoffs: Record package versions, random seeds and data provenance. Inspect missingness and assumptions before presenting a statistical result.
exercise: Create a reproducible report that separates raw data, transformations and interpretation.

role: Application developers, analysts and database engineers use SQL to define, query and modify relational data.
technical: Declarative queries describe results; the database planner selects an execution strategy. Constraints, transactions and indexes shape correctness and performance.
tradeoffs: Dialects differ. Use parameter binding for values, review query plans and understand transaction isolation. NULL introduces three-valued logic.
exercise: Design a reading-list schema with foreign keys and a parameterized query.

role: Host-application and game developers use Lua to make software scriptable without replacing its native core.
technical: A small embeddable language with dynamic types, tables, functions and coroutines. A C API connects the interpreter to its host.
tradeoffs: The host decides available capabilities. Sandbox untrusted scripts deliberately and control resource consumption and exposed APIs.
exercise: Embed a configuration script in a small host and validate the returned values.

role: Developers of concurrent services use Erlang processes and message passing to isolate work.
technical: Lightweight processes communicate through mailboxes. Links and monitors support failure observation; OTP adds reusable supervision and service patterns.
tradeoffs: Plan overload behavior, mailbox growth and recovery. Distribution does not remove partial failure or network partitions.
exercise: Model two communicating processes and test what happens when one stops.

role: Developers and researchers use Haskell to express transformations and domain models with strong static types.
technical: Pure functions, algebraic data types, type inference and non-strict evaluation are central. Effects are represented explicitly in typed interfaces.
tradeoffs: Laziness changes when work and allocation happen. Watch space use, make effects visible and keep abstractions understandable to the team.
exercise: Model a small domain with sum types and test pure transformations.
